title: Elizabeth Williams & Insight Housing: The Paper Trail
subtitle: From an Oakland ethics case to a publicly funded housing dispute
description: A source-tiered examination of Oakland Public Ethics Commission findings involving landlord Elizabeth Williams, and later allegations arising from an Insight Housing SSVF placement at an Oakland property associated with Williams.
caseReference: Oakland PEC Case No. 16-14 / ACCELA Case No. 2600830 / SSVF housing records / OPD report T26008570
keyPoints: In Oakland PEC Case No. 16-14, a hearing officer found that City building inspector Thomas Espinosa solicited and received four $300 payments from Elizabeth Williams in exchange for permit and inspection-related official acts.

The PEC findings describe Williams as an Oakland landlord whose properties had been the subject of multiple City maintenance lawsuits; the adjudicated ethics violations were findings against Espinosa, not a criminal judgment against Williams.

Press coverage of the Commission's final September 2021 decision reports the fine was increased to $309,600 across 47 violations, that Espinosa was separately paid to work as Williams's contractor while inspecting his own work, and that a second inspector, Anthony Harbaugh, was fined $55,000 for a related $300 payment and for failing to report income from Williams.
Oakland ACCELA Case No. 2600830, covering the exact SSVF placement property (1055 72nd Ave), is now directly confirmed as an open, unabated housing-habitability case.
In 2024, a veteran was placed through Insight Housing's SSVF program at an Oakland rental property associated with Williams, with public funding supporting the placement.

A 2026 Oakland Police Department report records allegations by the reporting party concerning housing conditions, program funds, eviction, and retaliation; those allegations are not treated in this episode as proven criminal conduct.

The episode asks what due diligence, inspection, complaint-handling, and fund-tracing controls should exist when public housing dollars intersect with a property or landlord already present in a municipal enforcement record.
investigativeAngles: Follow the property, permitting, inspection, and public-funding paper trail.
Separate adjudicated government findings from later complainant allegations.
Examine what screening and oversight existed before public funds supported the placement.
Identify gaps that require direct ACCELA, fire-inspection, SSVF ledger, and contracting records.
guestOpportunities: a municipal ethics or public-integrity attorney
a reporter experienced in public-contracting and homelessness funding
factCheckLayers: Tier 1: Oakland Public Ethics Commission Case No. 16-14 findings and exhibits

Tier 1: press coverage of the Commission's final decision and the separate Harbaugh matter (Oaklandside, CBS News/KPIX, East Bay Express), not yet reconciled against the Commission's own final written decision
Tier 1/2: court filings, agency correspondence, SSVF approval records, public-records responses, and the confirmed ACCELA Case No. 2600830 record
Tier 2: Oakland Police Department report T26008570 as proof an allegation was reported, not proof the allegation itself is true; reported FBI immunity for Williams (single-sourced)
Tier 3: complainant chronology and the single-sourced 2018 Indybay account of the 732 Apgar Street fire, where the underlying primary record has not yet been independently matched
